sentences.text: Cyamodus was a heavily armored swimmer with a turtle-like flat body covered in irregular hexagonal plates. Its heart-shaped skull supported large, rounded teeth adapted for crushing hard-shelled prey. The teeth resembled flat discs, with only one tooth in each premaxilla and two in each maxilla, while the largest teeth were located in the pterygoid. Unlike many reptiles, Cyamodus lacked dorsal spines but possessed a wing-like, elongated, flattened lateral spine that braced the subdermal carapace.
Most species measured between 1.3 and 1.5 meters in length and weighed 20 to 25 kilograms, though the smallest species, C. rostratus, was about 0.9 meters long and weighed only 5 kilograms.
The hexagonal plates on Cyamodus's shell increased protection and weight, an adaptation that helped it dive to reach shellfish.
Fossil evidence of two Cyamodus juveniles inside a Lariosaurus stomach suggests the species was vulnerable to predation.
The genus Cyamodus was named by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1863.
The first remains were found in shallow sea limestones of the Upper Muschelkalk near Bayreuth in Bavaria, Germany.
A complete skeleton of C. hildegardis, including the skull, was found outside the German Basin in the northern Tethys Sea in present-day Switzerland.
Six species of Cyamodus have been identified: C. rostratus, C. munsteri, C. tarnowitzensis, C. hildegardis, C. kuhnschneyderi, and C. orientalis.
Cyamodus was more agile than other single-shelled placodonts like Henodus, despite its cumbersome shell.

Cyamodus was initially thought to be an ancestral turtle but was later reclassified as a placodont related to other Triassic turtle-like reptiles. Once considered a possible ancestor of turtles due to its wide, flattened torso covered in dermal osteoderms, it is now considered a very distant relative. Later research determined that it was reclassified as a placodont and closely related to other Triassic turtle-like reptiles such as Henodus and Psephoderma.

Cyamodus belongs to the class Reptilia, the order Placodontia, suborder Sauropterygia, superfamily Cyamodontoidea, and family Cyamodontidae. The type species of the genus Cyamodus is Cyamodus muensteri.

While C.G. Diedrich suggested Cyamodus was an algae-grazer, this view is widely rejected by researchers like Torsten M. Scheyer, and the consensus remains that placodonts (except Henodus) were durophagous.
